name: Ikiki no Gomon (The Living Gate)

location.address: Oku-no-in (inner sanctuary) of Oyamazumi Shrine, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, open year round, no set hours. A public path/steps has been built through the hollow root passage itself. About a 5-minute walk from Oyamazumi Shrine's main hall; no dedicated parking at the site (nearest is the free municipal Fuji Park lot).
transport: Omishima Island, reached by car via the Shimanami Kaido (Omishima IC, about 10 minutes to the shrine) or by bus from Imabari Station (approx. 65 minutes to the Oyamazumi Shrine stop, then a 5-minute walk).
story:
There is a footpath through this tree. The split and hollowed base of the camphor forms a passage about two metres wide, three metres high and seven metres long, and worshippers walked through it on their way to the inner sanctuary of Oyamazumi Shrine. The name records exactly that: Ikiki no Gomon, the gate of the living tree.

How old it is depends on who you ask, and neither answer comes from a dating method anyone can check. The standard reference work on the island says 2,000 years. The board at the tree says 3,000. What has actually been measured is the size: eleven metres around the main trunk, fifteen and a half where the trunks meet, and thirty-two metres around the exposed root mass at ground level, which is the part you walk through.

It nearly died in the Meiji era, and its own believers were the reason. Bark taken from it was used as a charm for long life, stripped away until the original trunk was failing. The tree recovered the only way a camphor can, throwing fresh growth from its own root base. That second trunk, four and a half metres round, carries the crown today while the original stands spent beside it. One organism, regrown from itself.

Ehime Prefecture listed it as a Natural Monument in 1951. It sits five minutes from the shrine's main hall on Omishima, free and open at any hour, a short detour off the Shimanami Kaido.

name: Kawatana no Kusu no Mori (The Camphor Forest of Kawatana)

location.address: 6895 Kawatana-Shitaono, Toyoura-cho, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, publicly viewable. Reached in about 10 minutes by taxi/car from Kawatana Onsen Station (JR San-in Main Line), or about 20-30 minutes by car from the Chugoku Expressway (Kozuki IC or Shimonoseki IC). No fee or set hours found on the official tourism pages. Note the tree has been fenced/cordoned off around its base during its recovery (see health note below), so visitors view it from a short distance rather than approach the trunk closely.
transport: 10 minutes by taxi from Kawatana Onsen Station, JR San-in Main Line.
story:
It is called the Camphor Forest of Kawatana and it is a single tree. Eighteen major limbs leave the trunk about five metres up, and the crown covers 58 metres east to west by 53 north to south, close to 180 metres around the edge of its own shade. From any distance it reads as a small wood.

Japan designated it a National Natural Monument in 1922 and counts it among the three great camphors of the country. The trunk measures 11.2 metres round, the tree stands 27 metres tall, and every source gives the age as over a thousand years with no method attached and no upper figure, so that is where it is left.

In July 2017 it began to die. It shed most of its foliage in one season, and the city, the prefecture and the national Agency for Cultural Affairs graded it severely poor, its roots largely rotted. The suspected cause has never been confirmed: fill dirt laid during work on the neighbouring park, starving the roots of oxygen. Since around 2021 new shoots and green leaves have been returning, tentatively, while restoration work continues. Go expecting a survivor rather than a full canopy.

The base is cordoned off, so you look at it from a few metres back. The warlord Ouchi Yoshitaka's horse Hibarige is said to be buried nearby and is enshrined as a deity, remembered every 28 March. Ten minutes by taxi from Kawatana Onsen station, free, no gate and no hours.
